comparison: Both strongly support the core computational model findings (C6-C7, C30, C37-C43). OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic description and independence from ensemble size (C44), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the model 'convincingly shows' drift through excitability changes and Hebbian plasticity. High agreement on this central result.

Perfect alignment on robustness claims (C54-C56). Both evaluations support that alternative implementations (slope-based and threshold-based excitability changes) produce similar results. Peer reviewers note this successfully addressed concerns about model specificity.

Complete agreement on multi-memory extension (C62-C67). Both evaluations support that the model successfully maintains two distinct memories with independent drift and temporal decoding. Peer reviewers note this was added in response to their request and accept it without critique.

Full agreement on positioning relative to recent literature (C78-C81). Both evaluations support the framing that the model addresses firing rate drift and is consistent with time-driven mechanisms. No challenges from either evaluation.

Both mark as UNCERTAIN/SUPPORTED respectively for speculative extensions (C82-C85). OpenEval notes these mechanisms aren't directly tested in the model, while peer reviewers accept them as reasonable implications supported by citations. Mild divergence in confidence level.

Perfect agreement on scope and limitations (C86-C87). Both evaluations support the characterization as proof-of-principle work requiring experimental validation. Peer reviewers explicitly call it 'an important theoretical study' and 'important contribution.'

Both support decreasing correlation and perfect day decoder performance (C45-C48). OpenEval emphasizes the logical inference about temporal information (C47), while peer reviewers confirm 'perfect accuracy' in day classification. Strong agreement on these decoder results.

Both strongly support the non-trivial finding about intermediate excitability enabling temporal decoding (C10, C52-C53, C69). Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'interesting, and as the authors point out, not trivial.' OpenEval also covers additional claims (C8-C9, C31-C32) about drift gradualness.

Both support read-out mechanism findings (C11, C33, C57-C60). OpenEval emphasizes consistency with prior work and relationship between drift rate and read-out quality (C61). Peer reviewers accept the result but note the mechanism is 'trivial' given the learning rule construction. Agreement on support but different emphasis on novelty.

Both address speculative cognitive implications (C71-C72, C75-C77). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN noting claims go beyond model demonstrations, while peer reviewers SUPPORT as consistent with results and literature. OpenEval is more cautious about mental time-travel and memory linking claims.

Partial overlap on mechanistic claims. OpenEval R9 covers synthesis of main conclusions (C68, C73-C74, C76) marked SUPPORTED. Peer R2 focuses specifically on mechanistic explanation (C8, C73) also marked SUPPORTED. Both accept the core mechanism but OpenEval addresses broader time-stamping interpretation.

Both address sufficiency of excitability changes. OpenEval R9 supports time-stamping interpretation (C68, C74, C76) as reasonable inference. Peer R10 marks UNCERTAIN (C5, C29, C32, C68, C74) noting unresolved question about whether excitability alone is sufficient without global input structure. Significant divergence on confidence.

Minimal overlap on mechanistic explanation (C8). OpenEval R5 addresses broader temporal decoding findings while peer R2 focuses specifically on the mechanism of high excitability subset becoming more activated and connected. Both support the mechanistic explanation.

Partial overlap on drift gradualness and decoder performance (C9, C31). OpenEval R5 emphasizes temporal decoding at intermediate excitability, while peer R3 focuses on information preservation and day classification. Both support overlapping claims but address different aspects.
Minimal overlap on ensemble size independence (C44). OpenEval R3 includes this as part of core model findings, while peer R8 addresses it separately with implicit acceptance. Both support the claim.

Minimal overlap on drift rate and read-out quality relationship (C61). OpenEval R7 includes this as part of read-out mechanism findings, while peer R9 addresses it separately without challenge. Both support the claim.

OpenEval R1 addresses background claims about drift phenomenon and knowledge gaps (C1-C3, C12-C16, C19) marked SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory/background claims.

OpenEval R2 addresses background on excitability's role in memory allocation (C4, C20-C29) marked SUPPORTED. Distinguishes established facts from hypotheses. No direct peer review evaluation of these background claims, though peer R10 touches on C5 and C29 in context of sufficiency questions.

OpenEval R13 addresses summary of established findings from prior work (C17-C18, C34-C36) marked SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual/literature summary claims.
